name: Coenzyme Q10
lead: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10, ubiquinone, ubidecarenone) is a lipid-soluble benzoquinone that the human body makes and that is also found in meat, fish, seed oils and some vegetables [1]. It is a cofactor in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, where it supports ATP production, and it also acts as a membrane antioxidant [1][2]. People interested in appearance meet it in two main places: as an ingredient in anti-ageing creams and serums, where it is added to support the energy and antioxidant defences of skin cells, and as an oral supplement taken for energy, heart and mitochondrial support, often by people who train hard or take statins [9][7][22].

The skin rationale runs in a chain. CoQ10 levels in tissue are described as falling with age and external stress, and topical formulations are intended to raise the amount present in the outer and deeper skin layers, offset oxidative damage and so soften the visible signs of ageing such as wrinkle depth [9]. A 2024 review of 36 publications reported that ex vivo and in vivo studies showed raised CoQ10 in the stratum corneum and deeper layers and that clinical formulations reduced wrinkle depth [9]. A 2021 systematic review of over-the-counter topical anti-ageing agents covers it among other ingredients [11].

Outside skincare, CoQ10 has a large clinical literature. The Q-SYMBIO randomised trial in heart failure, trials in migraine and early Parkinson's disease, and meta-analyses on fatigue and fertility have all been published, while Cochrane reviews have reached cautious conclusions on cardiovascular outcomes [3][4][5][13][6][1]. It is sold as a dietary supplement and, according to Wikipedia, is not approved by the US FDA for treating any medical condition [1].

paras: CoQ10 consists of a benzoquinone head and a tail of ten isoprene units. In its pure form it is an orange lipophilic powder that does not dissolve in water [1]. Ubiquinone is the name chosen by the IUPAC-IUB commission in 1975 because the molecule is found from bacteria to humans [1]. In mitochondria it carries electrons between complexes of the respiratory chain; it is also found in other cell membranes and takes part in proton and calcium transport [1][2].

Coenzyme Q exists in three redox states: fully oxidised ubiquinone, a semiquinone radical, and fully reduced ubiquinol. It can carry two electrons or one, which suits both electron transport and radical scavenging, and it is also described as regenerating other antioxidants such as vitamin E [1]. Supplemental ubiquinone is reduced to ubiquinol during or after absorption in the small intestine [1]. Ubiquinol, the more polar electron-rich form, is sold as a separate supplement; Wikipedia's ubiquinol article suggests its extra hydrogens may help explain better reported bioavailability and notes that ubiquinol also occurs in food, accounting for 46 percent of CoQ10 intake in one Japanese diet analysis [29].

Most human tissues make CoQ10 in three stages: building the benzoquinone head from phenylalanine or tyrosine, building the isoprene tail from acetyl-CoA, and joining the two. At least 15 genes are required, and mutations in any of them, including PDSS1, PDSS2, COQ2 and COQ8A, can cause CoQ10 deficiency [1]. Primary deficiency can cause serious disease, for example steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in some patients with COQ gene mutations [1][10]. Plasma measurements reflect dietary intake rather than tissue status, so clinical centres typically measure CoQ10 in cultured skin fibroblasts, muscle biopsies or blood mononuclear cells [1].

Wikipedia, drawing on a 2010 food analysis, lists vegetable oils, meat and fish as rich sources, with soybean oil at 54 to 280 mg per kg, olive oil 40 to 160, beef heart 113 and red-flesh mackerel 43 to 67, while most fruits contain about 1 mg per kg and dairy is a comparatively poor source [1]. Estimated daily intake in the developed world is about 3 to 6 mg, mostly from meat, and frying reduces CoQ10 content by 14 to 32 percent [1]. CoQ10 is not classed as an essential nutrient and has no recommended intake level [1].

A small amount of the compound was isolated from horse intestinal lining in 1950 and called substance SA. In 1957 Crane and colleagues isolated it from beef heart mitochondrial membranes and named it Q-275; work showed it transports electrons within mitochondria [1]. In 1958 Morton renamed it ubiquinone because it appeared in nearly every animal tissue, and Wolf reported its full chemical structure the same year [1]. In 1966 Mellors and Tappel reported that a reduced quinone acts as an effective antioxidant in cells [1].

The skin literature developed from the idea that antioxidants in skin deplete under sunlight and age; Wikipedia cites 1990s and 2000 papers on antioxidants in human skin and on CoQ10 in nutrition and cosmetics as part of that background [1]. Over the following decades CoQ10 became a common cream ingredient and, according to a 2020 review, the third most consumed dietary supplement [15].

In cosmetics CoQ10 is added to anti-ageing creams, serums and eye products for its antioxidant role and its part in skin cell energy metabolism [9][1]. A 2024 review in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology searched PubMed for CoQ10, skin and ageing, retained 36 publications, and concluded that topical CoQ10 may raise cellular CoQ10, support energy metabolism, reduce free radicals and reduce visible signs of ageing, with clinical formulations reducing wrinkle depth [9]. A 2021 systematic review lists it in the broader class of over-the-counter topical anti-ageing agents [11].

Taken by mouth, CoQ10 is sometimes included in skin and longevity stacks, though the research on oral supplementation centres on cardiovascular, neurological and fertility outcomes rather than skin [3][4][5][6].

Because CoQ10 sits in the pathway that makes muscle cells' energy, lifters and people on testosterone therapy sometimes add it for energy and heart support, and as a companion to statins [7][22][23][24]. A 2022 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials with 1,126 participants reported a statistically significant reduction in fatigue scores with CoQ10 versus placebo (Hedges' g about -0.40), with the effect seen in both healthy and diseased participants [13]. Fatigue reduction is the route by which proponents link CoQ10 to better training capacity and, over time, physique.

CoQ10 has been studied as an adjunct in heart failure, myocardial infarction, migraine prevention, Parkinson's disease, fatigue, fertility in women with diminished ovarian reserve, kidney disease and several other conditions [3][12][4][5][13][6][14]. It is not an approved drug for these conditions [1].

CoQ10 is absorbed like other lipids, with bile and pancreatic enzymes forming micelles, and food, especially with fat, greatly enhances absorption. It travels in chylomicrons and lipoproteins and is excreted through bile and faeces [1]. After oral dosing the plasma peak occurs 6 to 8 hours later, sometimes with a second peak near 24 hours, and an elimination half-time of about 33 hours was found in a study using deuterium-labelled CoQ10 [1]. Because of its size and lipophilicity, bioavailability from supplements can be low; water-soluble and cyclodextrin formulations have been developed to improve it, while nanoparticle approaches have given inconsistent results [1][15].

For skin products the challenge is getting a large lipophilic molecule past the stratum corneum. The 2024 skin review reports that ex vivo and in vivo studies detected increased CoQ10 in the stratum corneum and deeper layers after topical application, and discusses formulation approaches intended to improve penetration [9].

Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme in CoQ10's synthesis pathway, and may reduce CoQ10 in blood [1]. Wikipedia states it is unclear whether they lower CoQ10 in muscle tissue and that the link to myopathy and rhabdomyolysis is controversial. A 2018 meta-analysis reported preliminary evidence that oral CoQ10 reduces statin-associated muscle symptoms, while 2015 and 2024 meta-analyses found no effect on statin myopathy [1].

Cardiovascular outcomes have been examined most. Wikipedia summarises that a 2014 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence on preventing heart disease, a 2016 Cochrane review found no effect on blood pressure, and a 2021 Cochrane review found no convincing evidence to support or refute use in heart failure, while a 2017 meta-analysis of heart failure patients reported about 31 percent lower mortality and better exercise capacity at 30 to 100 mg per day [1]. A 2023 meta-analysis in older people found a cardiovascular effect for ubiquinone but not for ubiquinol [1]. The Q-SYMBIO trial randomised patients with moderate to severe heart failure to CoQ10 or placebo on top of standard therapy for two years; 16-week measures did not change significantly, but major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 15 percent of the CoQ10 group versus 26 percent of the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.50), and the authors reported lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality [3].

A randomised trial published in Neurology in 2005 tested CoQ10 for migraine prophylaxis [4], and a dose-ranging trial in early Parkinson's disease reported evidence of slowing of functional decline [5]. A 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined fatigue [13], and a 2024 meta-analysis of six randomised trials in 1,529 women with diminished ovarian reserve undergoing IVF or ICSI found pretreatment associated with higher clinical pregnancy rate and more oocytes retrieved [6]. A crossover trial tested CoQ10 and nicotinamide riboside in chronic kidney disease [14], and a study examined CoQ10 and macrophage-mediated inflammation in the heart after myocardial infarction [12].

On the skin, the evidence base consists of the 2024 narrative review of 36 publications, which reported reduced wrinkle depth with clinical formulations, and the 2021 systematic review of topical anti-ageing agents [9][11]. Registered trials include studies in male infertility, polycystic ovary syndrome, lupus in children, cyclic vomiting syndrome, geriatric bipolar depression and ageing-related symptoms [16][17][18][19][20][21].

Oral CoQ10 is generally well tolerated. Reported effects are mostly gastrointestinal, such as nausea and abdominal pain, along with rashes and headaches, and doses of 100 to 300 mg per day have been associated with insomnia or elevated liver enzymes; an observed-safe-level assessment found the evidence acceptable at intakes up to 1,200 mg per day [1]. Caution is advised in bile duct obstruction, pregnancy and breastfeeding [1].

CoQ10 may inhibit the anticoagulant effect of warfarin, probably because of structural similarity to vitamin K and effects on cytochrome P450 enzymes, and may affect theophylline, so it is not recommended for people taking warfarin [1]. A forum user asked about drug interactions before trying a CoQ10 protocol while on several heart-rhythm medicines [22]. Wikipedia notes that manufacture of CoQ10 supplements is not regulated, so brands and batches may differ significantly [1].

The US FDA has not approved CoQ10 for treating any medical condition; it is sold as a dietary supplement, which is not subject to the same rules as medicinal drugs, and as an ingredient in some cosmetics and energy drinks [1].

On T Nation, CoQ10 is most often raised alongside statins, with users recommending pairing a statin with CoQ10 and a long thread about cholesterol theory describing statins as blocking CoQ10 production, which these posters said might affect the heart and muscle [7][8]. It is also mentioned in testosterone-therapy bloodwork discussions, in a mitochondrial protocol thread, and in a longevity thread as a supplement with supposedly great benefits [23][24][22][25]. A writer notes that most cardiologists react poorly when patients mention supplements other than fish oil or CoQ10 [26]. Users also post laboratory CoQ10 results with reference ranges [27][28].

Related entries include other skin antioxidants such as vitamin C and vitamin E, mitochondrial supplements such as nicotinamide riboside (examined with CoQ10 in a kidney disease crossover trial [14]), and fish oil, which forum users often pair with CoQ10 [26][25].

lore.intro: In training and testosterone-therapy forums CoQ10 is discussed chiefly as a companion to statins and a general heart and mitochondrial supplement, while in skincare it is marketed as an antioxidant cream ingredient [7][22][8][9].

claims.claim: Statins deplete CoQ10, so users should take it with them
claims.believers: Posters recommend coupling a statin with CoQ10 because statins interfere with its production [7][8].
claims.experts: Statins may lower blood CoQ10, but it is unclear whether muscle levels fall, and meta-analyses disagree on whether supplements reduce statin muscle symptoms [1].

claims.believers: Forum users take it with fish oil as a heart supplement [26][25].
claims.experts: Cochrane reviews found insufficient or no convincing evidence for prevention or treatment, while Q-SYMBIO and a 2017 meta-analysis reported lower mortality in heart failure [1][3].

claims.claim: Topical CoQ10 reduces wrinkles and slows skin ageing
claims.believers: Anti-ageing creams include CoQ10 for its antioxidant role and cellular energy support [9].
claims.experts: A 2024 review reported raised skin CoQ10 and reduced wrinkle depth with clinical formulations; it is a narrative review of 36 publications, and the 2021 systematic review treats it as one of many topical agents [9][11].

claims.claim: It provides mitochondrial energy support for fatigue and ageing
claims.believers: Users use it in mitochondrial protocols and longevity regimens [22][25].
claims.experts: A meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials reported reduced fatigue scores versus placebo, and CoQ10 has an established role in ATP production [13][2].

claims.claim: Ubiquinol is a better form than ubiquinone
claims.believers: Supplement marketing describes ubiquinol as the more bioavailable form.
claims.experts: Wikipedia's ubiquinol article suggests the reduced form's polarity may help absorption, and a 2023 meta-analysis in older people found a cardiovascular effect for ubiquinone but not ubiquinol [29][1].

claims.believers: Supplement users often discuss taking CoQ10 with a meal containing fat.
claims.experts: Pharmacokinetic summaries report that food, especially fat, greatly enhances absorption of this lipophilic molecule, and formulation research aims to improve low bioavailability [1][15].

chain: Topical or oral CoQ10 supplies a cofactor and antioxidant found in skin cells
Cellular energy metabolism and oxidative stress are the targets
Aim: smoother skin with shallower-looking wrinkles
angle.text: CoQ10 is used in creams and serums aiming for smoother, fresher-looking skin, and as a pill by people seeking more energy for training or heart support. The skin route is the more direct appearance use; the oral route is mostly a general-wellbeing and recovery chain.
